questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse see first?

options.text: A client with COPD whose oxygen saturation is 90% on 2 L/min by nasal cannula
A client one day after an appendectomy who rates pain 4 out of 10
A client who received IV morphine 20 minutes ago and is now difficult to rouse with a respiratory rate of 8/min
A client with type 2 diabetes whose pre-lunch glucose is 180 mg/dL

rationale.correct: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is an immediate threat to airway and breathing, so this client is the priority.

perOption.a: A saturation of 88% to 92% is an acceptable target for many clients with COPD; this client is stable.
perOption.b: Moderate pain one day after surgery is expected and can be managed after the unstable client is seen.
perOption.c: Sedation with a respiratory rate of 8/min after an opioid signals respiratory depression; the nurse must assess and support breathing now.
perOption.d: Mild hyperglycemia before a meal needs follow-up but is not life-threatening.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Use airway, breathing and circulation to choose which client to see first.

questions.stem: A client is diagnosed with Clostridioides difficile infection. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Place the client on contact precautions and wash hands with soap and water
Place the client on airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room
Wear a surgical mask whenever within 3 feet of the client
Use alcohol-based hand rub after each contact with the client

rationale.correct: C. difficile spreads by contact with spores, and alcohol does not kill spores, so contact precautions and soap-and-water hand washing are required.

perOption.a: Contact precautions and soap and water remove C. difficile spores from hands.
perOption.b: Airborne precautions are for organisms such as tuberculosis, measles and varicella.
perOption.c: Droplet precautions (a mask) are for organisms such as influenza; C. difficile is not spread by droplets.
perOption.d: Alcohol-based rub does not destroy C. difficile spores.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Match the isolation precautions and hand hygiene method to how the organism spreads.

questions.stem: A client who plans to become pregnant asks when to start taking folic acid. What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Start at least one month before you try to conceive."
"Start as soon as you have a positive pregnancy test."
"Start at the beginning of the second trimester."
"You only need it if a previous baby had a neural tube defect."

rationale.correct: The neural tube closes in the first weeks after conception, often before pregnancy is known, so folic acid should be taken before conception.

perOption.a: Taking folic acid before conception means levels are adequate when the neural tube forms.
perOption.b: By the time a pregnancy test is positive, neural tube development may already be under way.
perOption.c: The neural tube closes in the first trimester, so starting in the second trimester is too late.
perOption.d: All people who could become pregnant are advised to take folic acid; a history of neural tube defects calls for a higher dose.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects only when taken before and early in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A client on the medical unit tells the nurse, "I have a plan to end my life tonight." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Stay with the client and arrange continuous one-to-one observation
Call the client's family to come and sit with the client
Document the statement in the client's record
Ask the client to sign a no-harm contract

rationale.correct: A client with a specific plan is at high risk; the first priority is safety, which means the client is not left alone.

perOption.a: Continuous observation keeps the client safe while further help is arranged.
perOption.b: Family may support the client later, but the nurse must not leave the client alone to arrange this.
perOption.c: Documentation is required but does not protect the client.
perOption.d: No-harm contracts do not prevent suicide and are not a substitute for observation.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: A client who states a suicide plan needs immediate safety measures before anything else.

questions.stem: A client is receiving continuous enteral feedings through a nasogastric tube. How should the nurse position the client?

options.text: Head of the bed raised at least 30 degrees
Head of the bed raised 10 degrees
Prone with the head turned to the side

rationale.correct: Raising the head of the bed at least 30 degrees during and after feedings reduces the risk of aspiration.

perOption.a: At least 30 degrees uses gravity to keep the feeding in the stomach.
perOption.b: Lying flat increases reflux and aspiration.
perOption.c: 10 degrees is not high enough to reduce aspiration risk.
perOption.d: The prone position puts pressure on the abdomen and increases reflux.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or more for clients receiving tube feedings.

questions.stem: An adult client is due for digoxin 0.125 mg. The apical pulse is 52/min. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the dose and notify the healthcare provider
Give the dose and recheck the pulse in one hour

rationale.correct: Digoxin slows the heart rate; an apical pulse below 60/min in an adult is a reason to hold the dose and report it.

perOption.a: Holding the dose avoids further slowing of the heart and lets the provider assess for toxicity.
perOption.b: Giving the dose may slow the heart rate further.
perOption.c: Nurses do not change a prescribed dose without an order.
perOption.d: Food does not change the drug's effect on heart rate.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Check the apical pulse for a full minute before giving digoxin and hold it for an adult rate below 60/min.

questions.stem: Which laboratory result does the nurse use to monitor the effect of warfarin?

rationale.correct: Warfarin's effect is monitored with the PT/INR.

perOption.a: The INR measures warfarin's anticoagulant effect; a common target is 2 to 3.
perOption.b: The aPTT is used to monitor unfractionated heparin.
perOption.c: The platelet count is watched for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, not to adjust warfarin.
perOption.d: Hemoglobin A1c reflects average blood glucose.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Know which coagulation test goes with each anticoagulant.

questions.stem: A client received IV contrast for a CT scan. Which laboratory value is most important for the nurse to monitor over the next 48 hours?

rationale.correct: Contrast can injure the kidneys, and a rising serum creatinine is the main sign of contrast-associated kidney injury.

perOption.a: Creatinine rises when kidney filtration falls.
perOption.b: ALT reflects liver injury, which contrast does not usually cause.
perOption.c: Amylase reflects pancreatic injury.
perOption.d: Troponin reflects heart muscle injury.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor kidney function after a client receives iodinated contrast.

questions.stem: A client has a chest tube connected to a water-seal drainage system. The nurse sees continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber. What does this finding suggest?

options.text: An air leak in the system
The system is working as expected

rationale.correct: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber means air is entering the system all the time, from a leak in the tubing or connections or from the client's lung.

perOption.a: Continuous bubbling points to an air leak that the nurse should locate.
perOption.b: Gentle bubbling only on exhalation or coughing can be expected with a pneumothorax; continuous bubbling is not.
perOption.c: A clamped tube would stop bubbling, not cause it.
perOption.d: When the lung has re-expanded, bubbling stops.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell expected from unexpected findings in a chest drainage system.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is shaky and sweaty, with a blood glucose of 55 mg/dL. The client is alert and can swallow. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Give 15 g of a fast-acting carbohydrate, such as 4 oz of juice
Give the scheduled dose of rapid-acting insulin
Recheck the blood glucose in one hour

rationale.correct: For an alert client who can swallow, hypoglycemia is treated with 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate, then the glucose is rechecked in 15 minutes.

perOption.a: Fast-acting carbohydrate raises the glucose quickly and is safe in a client who can swallow.
perOption.b: Insulin would lower the glucose further.
perOption.c: Glucagon is for clients who are unconscious or cannot swallow safely.
perOption.d: Waiting an hour leaves the hypoglycemia untreated; recheck after 15 minutes of treatment.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the 15-15 rule for a conscious client with hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: The nurse is assigning care for a stable client to assistive personnel. Which tasks are appropriate to delegate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Helping the client walk in the hall
Teaching the client to self-inject insulin
Evaluating the client's response to pain medication

rationale.correct: Assistive personnel can do routine, standard tasks for stable clients; assessment, teaching and evaluation stay with the nurse.

perOption.a: Measuring vital signs on a stable client is a routine task.
perOption.b: Helping a stable client walk is within the role of assistive personnel.
perOption.c: Admission assessment requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated.
perOption.d: Teaching is a nursing responsibility.
perOption.e: Measuring and recording intake and output is a routine task.
perOption.f: Evaluating a response to medication requires nursing judgment.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Delegate tasks, not assessment, teaching or evaluation.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Place the client in a negative-pressure (airborne infection isolation) room
Wear a fitted N95 respirator when entering the room
Have the client wear a surgical mask when leaving the room
Keep the door open so the client can be observed
Place the client in a shared room with another client who has pneumonia

rationale.correct: Tuberculosis spreads by airborne droplet nuclei, so the client needs airborne precautions.

perOption.a: A negative-pressure room keeps airborne particles from leaving the room.
perOption.b: An N95 respirator filters the small particles that carry tuberculosis.
perOption.c: A surgical mask on the client reduces the spread of particles during transport.
perOption.d: The door must stay closed so negative pressure is maintained.
perOption.e: A client with suspected tuberculosis needs a private airborne isolation room.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Use airborne precautions for tuberculosis.

questions.stem: Which developmental milestones does the nurse expect in a healthy 6-month-old infant? Select all that apply.

options.text: Passes a toy from one hand to the other
Picks up small objects with a pincer grasp

rationale.correct: Rolling over, sitting with support and passing objects between hands are typical by about 6 months.

perOption.a: Most infants roll from back to front by about 6 months.
perOption.b: Infants usually sit with support by 6 months and without support by about 7 to 8 months.
perOption.c: Transferring objects between hands appears at about 6 months.
perOption.d: Independent walking typically begins at about 12 months.
perOption.e: The pincer grasp develops at about 9 to 10 months.
perOption.f: Two-word phrases usually appear at about 2 years.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the expected milestones of infancy.

questions.stem: A client who drinks alcohol daily was admitted 18 hours ago. Which findings suggest alcohol withdrawal? Select all that apply.

rationale.correct: Alcohol withdrawal causes autonomic hyperactivity, usually starting 6 to 24 hours after the last drink.

perOption.a: Tremors are an early sign of withdrawal.
perOption.b: Sweating reflects autonomic hyperactivity.
perOption.c: Tachycardia reflects autonomic hyperactivity.
perOption.d: Withdrawal raises the heart rate; bradycardia is not expected.
perOption.e: Anxiety and agitation are common in withdrawal.
perOption.f: Pinpoint pupils suggest opioid use, not alcohol withdrawal.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the early signs of alcohol withdrawal.

questions.stem: Which actions help prevent pressure injuries in a client on bed rest? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours
Keep the skin clean and dry
Massage reddened areas over bony prominences
Keep the head of the bed above 45 degrees at all times

rationale.correct: Relieving pressure, protecting the skin from moisture and spreading pressure over a larger area prevent pressure injuries.

perOption.a: Regular repositioning relieves pressure on tissues.
perOption.b: Moisture weakens skin and increases breakdown.
perOption.c: Pressure-redistributing surfaces lower pressure on bony areas.
perOption.d: Massaging reddened areas can damage the tissue further.
perOption.e: A high head of the bed increases shear on the sacrum; keep it at 30 degrees or lower when possible.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose evidence-based measures to prevent pressure injuries.

questions.stem: A client started lisinopril two weeks ago. Which findings should the nurse report to the healthcare provider? Select all that apply.

options.text: Swelling of the lips and tongue

rationale.correct: ACE inhibitors can cause cough, angioedema and hyperkalemia; these need to be reported.

perOption.a: A dry cough is a common ACE-inhibitor effect that may lead the provider to change the drug.
perOption.b: Angioedema can block the airway and is an emergency.
perOption.c: ACE inhibitors raise potassium; 5.9 mEq/L is above the normal range.
perOption.d: This blood pressure shows the drug is working.
perOption.e: A heart rate of 72/min is normal.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Monitor for the serious adverse effects of ACE inhibitors.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing to give potassium chloride intravenously. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Give it with an infusion pump
Give it by IV push over 1 minute
Check that the client's urine output is adequate first
Monitor the IV site for pain and phlebitis
Add it to an IV bag that is already hanging

rationale.correct: IV potassium must be diluted, given slowly with a pump, and given only when the kidneys can excrete it.

perOption.a: A pump controls the rate and prevents a dangerous bolus.
perOption.b: IV push potassium can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias.
perOption.c: Potassium is excreted by the kidneys, so poor urine output risks hyperkalemia.
perOption.d: Potassium irritates veins, so the site must be watched.
perOption.e: Adding potassium to a hanging bag can leave it poorly mixed and deliver a concentrated dose.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Give IV potassium safely.

questions.stem: A client had a cardiac catheterization through the femoral artery 2 hours ago. Which findings could indicate bleeding? Select all that apply.

options.text: A firm swelling at the insertion site
A warm foot with a strong pedal pulse

rationale.correct: Bleeding after femoral access can be external, a hematoma, or retroperitoneal, and causes signs of hypovolemia.

perOption.a: A firm swelling suggests a hematoma.
perOption.b: Tachycardia is an early compensation for blood loss.
perOption.c: Hypotension can follow significant blood loss.
perOption.d: Back or flank pain can signal retroperitoneal bleeding.
perOption.e: A heart rate of 64/min is not a sign of bleeding.
perOption.f: A warm foot with a strong pulse shows good circulation to the limb.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize signs of bleeding after femoral arterial access.

questions.stem: Which findings are consistent with left-sided heart failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shortness of breath when lying flat

rationale.correct: Left-sided failure backs blood up into the lungs, causing pulmonary congestion.

perOption.a: Fluid in the alveoli causes crackles.
perOption.b: Orthopnea results from pulmonary congestion when lying flat.
perOption.c: Pink, frothy sputum is a sign of pulmonary edema.
perOption.d: Jugular venous distension is a sign of right-sided failure.
perOption.e: Dependent edema is a sign of right-sided failure.
perOption.f: Hepatomegaly is a sign of right-sided failure.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell left-sided from right-sided heart failure by where fluid backs up.

questions.stem: Which findings does the nurse expect in a client with diabetic ketoacidosis? Select all that apply.

options.text: A fruity odor on the breath

rationale.correct: Diabetic ketoacidosis combines hyperglycemia, ketosis and metabolic acidosis.

perOption.a: Kussmaul respirations blow off carbon dioxide to compensate for acidosis.
perOption.b: Acetone from ketones gives the breath a fruity odor.
perOption.c: Severe hyperglycemia, usually above 250 mg/dL, is expected.
perOption.d: A pH of 7.48 is alkalosis; DKA causes acidosis (pH below 7.35).
perOption.e: High glucose causes osmotic diuresis and frequent urination.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the cues of diabetic ketoacidosis.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client 12 hours after a total thyroidectomy. Select the 3 findings that require immediate follow-up.

options.text: Tingling around the mouth and in the fingertips
Facial twitching when the cheek is tapped

rationale.correct: Damage to the parathyroid glands causes hypocalcemia (tingling, a positive Chvostek sign), and stridor signals airway obstruction; all three need action now.

perOption.a: Perioral and fingertip tingling is an early sign of hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury.
perOption.b: Mild hoarseness is common after thyroid surgery because of laryngeal edema and usually resolves.
perOption.c: Stridor signals airway narrowing from edema, bleeding or tetany and is an emergency.
perOption.d: Mild incision pain is expected and can be managed with the prescribed analgesic.
perOption.e: Facial twitching on tapping (Chvostek sign) indicates hypocalcemia.
perOption.f: A slightly raised temperature in the first 24 hours is expected after surgery.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: After thyroidectomy, watch for airway obstruction and hypocalcemia.

questions.stem: A client's serum potassium is 6.0 mEq/L. Select the 2 prescribed medications the nurse should clarify with the provider before giving.

rationale.correct: Spironolactone and lisinopril both raise serum potassium, so giving them during hyperkalemia could cause dangerous dysrhythmias.

perOption.a: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic and raises potassium further.
perOption.b: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that lowers potassium; it is not the concern here.
perOption.c: ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril reduce aldosterone and raise potassium.
perOption.d: Acetaminophen does not affect potassium.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Know which medications raise serum potassium.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with left-sided or right-sided heart failure.

rationale.correct: Left-sided failure backs blood up into the lungs; right-sided failure backs blood up into the systemic veins.

perOption.r1:c1: Crackles come from fluid in the lungs, typical of left-sided failure.
perOption.r1:c2: Right-sided failure congests the systemic veins, not the lungs.
perOption.r2:c1: Left-sided failure congests the pulmonary circulation, not the neck veins.
perOption.r2:c2: Jugular venous distension reflects systemic venous congestion from right-sided failure.
perOption.r3:c1: Peripheral edema is not the main sign of left-sided failure.
perOption.r3:c2: Dependent edema results from systemic venous congestion in right-sided failure.
perOption.r4:c1: Orthopnea occurs because lying flat increases pulmonary congestion in left-sided failure.
perOption.r4:c2: Breathlessness lying flat comes from lung congestion, which is left-sided.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell left-sided from right-sided heart failure by where fluid backs up.

questions.stem: A client with a new deep vein thrombosis is receiving a continuous heparin infusion. For each action, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.

rows.text: Massage the affected calf to relieve discomfort
Give the prescribed vitamin K with the heparin

rationale.correct: Care for DVT on heparin protects the clot from dislodging and monitors anticoagulation.

perOption.r1:c1: Massaging the leg can dislodge the clot and cause a pulmonary embolism.
perOption.r1:c2: Correct: massage is contraindicated because it can dislodge the clot.
perOption.r2:c1: Correct: the aPTT guides heparin dose adjustments.
perOption.r2:c2: The aPTT must be monitored; it is how heparin therapy is titrated.
perOption.r3:c1: Correct: elevation reduces swelling and promotes venous return.
perOption.r3:c2: Elevation is a standard comfort and circulation measure for DVT.
perOption.r4:c1: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin, and would work against anticoagulation.
perOption.r4:c2: Correct: vitamin K is not given with anticoagulation therapy; protamine reverses heparin.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Know the nursing care of a client with DVT receiving heparin.

questions.stem: For each medication, select the adverse effects the nurse should teach the client to report right away. Each medication may have more than one.

columns.text: Swelling of the face, lips or tongue
Muscle pain with weakness and trouble breathing

rationale.correct: Teaching focuses on the serious adverse effect of each drug: bleeding for warfarin, angioedema for lisinopril, lactic acidosis for metformin.

perOption.r1:c1: Bleeding is the main adverse effect of warfarin.
perOption.r1:c2: Angioedema is linked to ACE inhibitors, not warfarin.
perOption.r1:c3: This describes lactic acidosis, a metformin effect.
perOption.r1:c4: Tarry stools can signal gastrointestinal bleeding on warfarin.
perOption.r2:c2: ACE inhibitors can cause angioedema, which can block the airway.
perOption.r2:c3: This is not an effect of lisinopril.
perOption.r2:c4: Lisinopril does not cause gastrointestinal bleeding.
perOption.r3:c3: Muscle pain, weakness and trouble breathing can signal lactic acidosis from metformin.
perOption.r3:c4: Metformin does not cause gastrointestinal bleeding.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach clients the serious adverse effects of common medications.

questions.stem: For each type of transmission-based precautions, select the conditions that require it.

rationale.correct: Precautions match how the organism spreads: contact for C. difficile and MRSA, droplet for influenza, airborne for tuberculosis and measles.

perOption.r1:c1: Influenza is not spread by touch and contaminated surfaces; it needs droplet precautions.
perOption.r1:c2: Correct: Influenza is spread by large droplets within about 1 metre.
perOption.r1:c3: Influenza is not spread by small particles that stay in the air; it needs droplet precautions.
perOption.r2:c1: Correct: Clostridioides difficile is spread by touch and contaminated surfaces.
perOption.r2:c2: Clostridioides difficile is not spread by large droplets within about 1 metre; it needs contact precautions.
perOption.r2:c3: Clostridioides difficile is not spread by small particles that stay in the air; it needs contact precautions.
perOption.r3:c1: Pulmonary tuberculosis is not spread by touch and contaminated surfaces; it needs airborne precautions.
perOption.r3:c2: Pulmonary tuberculosis is not spread by large droplets within about 1 metre; it needs airborne precautions.
perOption.r3:c3: Correct: Pulmonary tuberculosis is spread by small particles that stay in the air.
perOption.r4:c1: Measles is not spread by touch and contaminated surfaces; it needs airborne precautions.
perOption.r4:c2: Measles is not spread by large droplets within about 1 metre; it needs airborne precautions.
perOption.r4:c3: Correct: Measles is spread by small particles that stay in the air.
perOption.r5:c1: Correct: MRSA wound infection is spread by touch and contaminated surfaces.
perOption.r5:c2: MRSA wound infection is not spread by large droplets within about 1 metre; it needs contact precautions.
perOption.r5:c3: MRSA wound infection is not spread by small particles that stay in the air; it needs contact precautions.

questions.stem: The nurse assesses a client 1 day after a total hip arthroplasty. For each body system, select the findings that require immediate follow-up.

options.text: Capillary refill under 3 seconds in the toes
Cool, pale foot on the operative side
Sudden shortness of breath and chest pain
Bright red drainage saturating the dressing
Operative leg shorter and turned outward

rationale.correct: After hip arthroplasty, watch for impaired circulation, pulmonary embolism, hemorrhage and dislocation.

perOption.a: Brisk capillary refill shows adequate perfusion.
perOption.b: A cool, pale foot suggests impaired arterial circulation.
perOption.c: Strong, equal pulses are a normal finding.
perOption.d: Sudden dyspnea and chest pain suggest a pulmonary embolism.
perOption.e: A saturation of 96% is within normal limits.
perOption.f: Clear breath sounds are a normal finding.
perOption.g: Saturating the dressing with bright red blood suggests hemorrhage.
perOption.h: Shortening and external rotation suggest hip dislocation.
perOption.i: Mild bruising is expected after surgery.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the complications of total hip arthroplasty.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with heart failure before discharge. For each topic, select the statements that show the client understands the teaching.

options.text: "I will keep my sodium to the amount my provider set."
"I can use as much salt substitute as I like."
"Canned soups are a good low-salt choice."
"I will weigh myself every morning after I urinate."
"I will call if I gain more than 1 kg (2 lb) in a day."
"I only need to check my weight at clinic visits."
"I should stay in bed most of the day."

rationale.correct: Heart failure self-care is a sodium limit, daily weights with prompt reporting of gains, and paced activity.

perOption.a: A prescribed sodium limit reduces fluid retention.
perOption.b: Salt substitutes contain potassium and can cause hyperkalemia with some heart failure drugs.
perOption.c: Canned soups are usually high in sodium.
perOption.d: Daily weights at the same time detect fluid retention early.
perOption.e: A rapid weight gain signals fluid retention and should be reported.
perOption.f: Weekly or monthly weights miss fluid gain until it is severe.
perOption.g: Pacing activity with rest reduces cardiac workload.
perOption.h: Bed rest causes deconditioning; gradual activity is encouraged.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate heart failure discharge teaching.

questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes is shaky, sweaty and anxious 2 hours after taking insulin and skipping lunch. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The client is most likely experiencing {{b1}}, as shown by {{b2}}.

options.text: a fruity odor on the breath

rationale.correct: Insulin without food leads to low glucose; shakiness and sweating are adrenergic signs, confirmed by a glucose below 70 mg/dL.

perOption.b1:a: Insulin with a missed meal and adrenergic symptoms point to hypoglycemia.
perOption.b1:b: Hyperglycemia causes thirst and polyuria, not shakiness and sweating.
perOption.b1:c: DKA develops over hours with ketosis; it does not follow a missed meal after insulin.
perOption.b2:a: A glucose of 52 mg/dL confirms hypoglycemia.
perOption.b2:b: A fruity breath odor suggests ketosis from DKA.
perOption.b2:c: Frequent urination is a sign of hyperglycemia.

references: SAMPLE CONTENT: written for development and testing, not reviewed by a nurse educator. Do not use for exam preparation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize hypoglycemia and its confirming finding.

questions.stem: The nurse discovers a small fire in a client's room. Complete the sentence.

content.template: The nurse should first {{b1}} and then {{b2}}.

options.text: move the client out of immediate danger
put out the fire with an extinguisher
take the client to the elevator

rationale.correct: Fire response follows RACE: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Extinguish.

perOption.b1:a: Rescue comes first: clients in immediate danger are moved.
perOption.b1:b: Extinguishing comes after rescue, alarm and containment.
perOption.b1:c: Calling the provider does not protect anyone from the fire.

questions.stem: For each medication, choose the assessment that matters most before giving it.

rationale.correct: Each check targets the drug's main risk: bradycardia for digoxin, hypotension and bradycardia for beta blockers, hypokalemia for loop diuretics.

perOption.b1:a: Digoxin slows the heart; hold it if the apical pulse is below 60/min.
perOption.b1:b: Digoxin has little effect on blood pressure; the apical rate is the key check.
perOption.b1:c: Potassium matters for digoxin toxicity, but the apical pulse is checked before every dose.

perOption.b3:a: Furosemide does not slow the heart.
perOption.b3:b: Blood pressure matters, but low potassium is the main risk of loop diuretics.
perOption.b3:c: Furosemide wastes potassium; hypokalemia can cause dysrhythmias.

questions.stem: A child weighing 17.3 kg is prescribed amoxicillin 25 mg/kg per dose. The suspension contains 250 mg in 5 mL. How many mL should the nurse give? Round to the nearest tenth.

rationale.correct: Dose = 17.3 kg × 25 mg/kg = 432.5 mg. Volume = 432.5 mg ÷ 50 mg/mL = 8.65 mL, which rounds to 8.7 mL.

questions.stem: Place the steps for giving eye drops in order.

items.text: Pull the lower lid down to form a pocket
Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves
Press gently on the inner corner of the eye
Ask the client to tilt the head back and look up
Place the drops in the pocket of the lower lid

rationale.correct: Clean hands, position the client, make a pocket, instill the drops, then press on the inner canthus to limit systemic absorption.

perOption.a: Hand hygiene comes first to prevent infection.
perOption.b: Looking up moves the cornea away from the dropper.
perOption.c: The pocket receives the drops instead of the sensitive cornea.
perOption.d: Drops go into the conjunctival sac, not onto the cornea.
perOption.e: Pressure on the inner canthus reduces drainage into the nasolacrimal duct.

questions.stem: The nurse finds an adult client unresponsive in bed. Place the actions in order.

items.text: Call for help and activate the emergency response
Attach the defibrillator when it arrives
Check for breathing and a pulse for no more than 10 seconds

rationale.correct: Basic life support: confirm unresponsiveness, call for help, check breathing and pulse, start compressions, then defibrillate as soon as possible.

perOption.a: Confirm the client is unresponsive before acting.
perOption.b: Calling for help early brings the team and the defibrillator.
perOption.c: A pulse and breathing check of up to 10 seconds avoids delaying CPR.
perOption.d: Compressions start immediately when there is no pulse.
perOption.e: The defibrillator is attached as soon as it is available.
